prompt: Why does shop.sql compute every value from the row's number instead of calling random()?
hint: Think about comparing your screen with the course's.

choices.text: random() is not available in PostgreSQL 16
choices.why: It exists. It was avoided on purpose.
Speed is not the reason; the load takes about fourteen seconds either way.

choices.text: So your numbers match the course's
choices.why: Right. Same rows, same numbers.

choices.text: Random values would break the foreign key
choices.why: A random customer between 1 and 50,000 would satisfy it just as well.

prompt: `\dt+` shows orders at 65 MB and `\di+` shows its three indexes at 12 MB, 9408 kB and 21 MB. What does that tell you?
hint: Add the indexes up.

choices.why: Nothing here suggests damage; this is the ordinary size of three B-tree indexes.
Right. About 42 MB of index for 65 MB of table.

choices.text: The table is mostly empty pages
choices.why: It was just loaded; there are no dead rows yet.
\dt+ shows the table without its indexes.

prompt: Put the steps to rebuild shop exactly as it was in order.
hint: Remove, make empty, fill.
trap: Running the file into an existing shop fails at the first CREATE TABLE: the tables are already there.

prompt: Match each entry of the data directory to what it holds.
hint: One per database, one shared, one log, one record of commits.

prompt: Right after loading shop, pg_wal was 337M and base was 153M. What is the right reading?
hint: Every change goes to the log first.

choices.text: Something is wrong: the log should never exceed the data
choices.why: After a bulk load it routinely does, for a while.

choices.text: The load went through the log first
choices.why: Right. Bounded, and lesson 7 says by what.

choices.text: The old segments are safe to delete now
choices.why: Never by hand. The server decides when a segment is no longer needed.

choices.text: pg_wal holds a second copy of every table
choices.why: It holds a record of changes, not copies of tables.

prompt: A server was killed with kill -9 and postmaster.pid is still in the data directory. What happens at the next start?
hint: The file records a process id.

choices.why: Right. The file only blocks a server that is really running.

choices.text: It refuses to start until somebody deletes the file
choices.why: It checks the process first; deleting the file by hand is the dangerous habit.

choices.text: It starts a second server beside the old one
choices.why: Two servers on one directory is exactly what the file exists to prevent.

choices.text: It recreates the cluster from scratch
choices.why: Nothing is recreated; crash recovery replays the log.

prompt: The file that records which major version made a data directory is called ___.
hint: Its name says it, in capitals.

prompt: What is the right way to find the file that holds a table?
hint: Ask the server.

choices.text: Look for a file named after the table under base/
choices.why: No file is named after a table.
Right. The number can change, so look it up each time.

choices.text: Take the newest file in the database's directory
choices.why: The newest file is whatever changed last, which tells you nothing about which table it is.
There is no arithmetic between the two numbers.

prompt: Which fork of a table appears only after the first VACUUM?
hint: Two bits per page.

choices.why: Right. VACUUM is what fills it in.
It holds the rows, so it exists from the first insert.
It was already there after the load.
An index is a relation of its own, not a fork of the table.

prompt: orders' main fork is 68,272,128 bytes and a page is 8192 bytes. How many pages does it hold?
hint: Divide.

prompt: Somebody asks how big orders is. Which function answers with the table, its maps and every index together?
hint: The one with total in its name.

choices.why: Right: 108 MB here.
That is the main fork alone: 65 MB.
That adds the maps and TOAST, but no index.
That is the indexes alone.

prompt: A table of 3.5 GB lives in base/16386. How many files hold its main fork?
hint: segment_size is 1GB.

choices.why: Right. Three full gigabytes and half of a fourth.
No file grows past segment_size.

choices.text: Three, and the remainder goes in the free space map
choices.why: The free space map holds no rows.

choices.text: It depends on the filesystem's block size
choices.why: The split is PostgreSQL's, fixed at compile time.

prompt: After TRUNCATE scratch, pg_relation_filepath gave a different number. Why is TRUNCATE instant on a table of any size?
hint: It did not touch the old rows.

choices.text: It marks every row deleted in one pass
choices.why: That is DELETE, and it takes time in proportion to the rows.

choices.text: It defers the work to the next VACUUM
choices.why: Nothing is left for VACUUM: the old file is gone at commit.

choices.text: It swaps in a new empty file
choices.why: Right. The oid stays; the relfilenode changes.
It would be just as fast at a billion rows.

prompt: On Ubuntu, where is pg_hba.conf for the cluster 16/main?
hint: Where every other service keeps its configuration.

choices.why: That is upstream's place, and the data directory.
That holds the programs.
Right. Debian and Ubuntu keep the data directory pure data.
That holds the socket.

prompt: You keep a second cluster for rehearsals and do not want it running after every reboot. What do you change?
hint: One word in one small file.

choices.why: That changes nothing about boot, and is never done by hand.
Right. auto, manual or disabled.

choices.text: Drop it with pg_dropcluster and recreate it when needed
choices.why: That deletes its data, configuration and log.
That holds extra options for pg_ctl, not whether it starts.

prompt: What does `sudo pg_dropcluster --stop 16 main` delete? Choose all that apply.
hint: The three places a cluster lives on Ubuntu.

choices.why: Yes, the data directory.
Yes, its configuration.
Yes, the log too.
The programs stay; pg_createcluster can make a new cluster at once.
Only the one named.

prompt: What does moving the configuration out of the data directory make possible?
hint: Think about replacing the data directory.

choices.text: Running two major versions from one data directory
choices.why: No data directory serves two major versions.

choices.text: Replacing the data, keeping the settings
choices.why: Right. The data directory becomes pure data.
The files still belong to postgres.
postmaster.pid is still written in the data directory.

prompt: What does ALTER TABLE customers SET TABLESPACE fast do while it runs?
hint: The files move.

choices.text: Changes a pointer; the files stay where they are
choices.why: The new path is in the new directory: the data was copied.

choices.text: Moves the table and all its indexes
choices.why: Only the table moved; each index needs its own ALTER INDEX.

choices.text: Copies the table in the background without locks
choices.why: It holds a lock that blocks everyone until the copy ends.
Right. Nothing for 4.5 MB, an outage for 200 GB.

prompt: How does the cluster remember where tablespace fast is after a restart?
hint: Look in pg_tblspc.

choices.text: A symbolic link in pg_tblspc, named by the tablespace's oid
choices.why: Right. It points at /srv/pg/fast.
No configuration was written.
fstab mounts disks; it knows nothing about tablespaces.
Nothing is scanned; the link is followed.

prompt: A cloud server has one network volume type for every disk. A colleague wants a tablespace for the hottest table. What is the strongest objection?
hint: What would the tablespace buy here?

choices.why: They are fully supported.

choices.text: A tablespace cannot hold an indexed table
choices.why: Tables and indexes both go in tablespaces.

choices.text: Only superusers may read a table in a tablespace
choices.why: Privileges are the same wherever the files are.

choices.text: There is no faster place to put it
choices.why: Right. All the cost, none of the gain.

prompt: The disk is nearly full and pg_wal is the biggest directory. What should you do first?
hint: The server decides which segments it still needs.

choices.text: Delete the oldest files in pg_wal
choices.why: The cluster may never start again.
The server would find segments it cannot read.
Right. Lesson 7 says why; lesson 24 writes the runbook.
Moving files by hand under the server is the same mistake.

prompt: Why is `cp -a` of a running server's data directory not a backup?
hint: The files change while cp reads them.

choices.text: cp cannot read files owned by postgres
choices.why: With sudo it reads them fine. The problem is when.

choices.text: The copy mixes moments that no recovery reconciles
choices.why: Right. Stopped, or with tools built for it.

choices.text: cp does not copy symbolic links
choices.why: -a copies them; that is not the problem.
Size has nothing to do with it.

prompt: A server refuses to start, saying another server may be running on the data directory. ps shows no postgres process. What is the right reading?
hint: Read the whole message before touching anything.

choices.why: If something else holds that pid, you have just allowed two servers on one directory.
Nothing is wrong with the programs.

choices.text: Read the log first, then check whose pid that is
choices.why: Right. The log names what it found, and that decides the next step.

choices.text: Change the data directory's permissions to 777
choices.why: The server would then refuse for a second reason.

prompt: The number a table's file carries on disk, which TRUNCATE changes while the table's oid stays, is its ___.
hint: Relation, file, node.

prompt: Match each question to the command that answers it.
hint: Server for meaning, shell for bytes.

pairs.left: Which file is the orders table?
How big is each part of the cluster?
Where does the cluster keep its log?
